title: Verifier‑Grounded Evaluation of LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: A Preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic Study
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) comparing a deterministic template baseline to a single‑pass LLM generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on N = 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks using a deterministic validator. Under the frozen confirmatory semantics (shared_initial_candidate per pair) all confirmatory episodes completed: baseline = 120/120 verifier passes; guarded (gpt‑5‑mini, seed_0) = 120/120 verifier passes. Paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We (i) publish the exact execution and analysis artifacts and SHA‑256 fingerprints required to reproduce the run (see execution/execution_manifest.json in the artifact bundle), (ii) diagnose—using archived artifacts—why the paired outcome is uninformative about independent generative reliability (preregistered shared_initial_candidate design, template‑tight task synthesis, and validator–task coupling), and (iii) provide artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory design, validator diversity, and expanded task heterogeneity) that preserve reproducibility while producing informative independent comparisons. The immutable initial master prompt is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

sections.introduction:
Automating NetOps by translating high‑level operator intent into device configurations promises substantial operational productivity gains but raises correctness and safety concerns: generated device commands must preserve reachability, enforce access control invariants, and respect transient safety constraints during multi‑step changes. Deterministic offline verifiers that compute the semantic effects of configurations (reachability, ACL enforcement, transient invariants) are a practical safety net widely used for pre‑deployment validation; they provide an objective oracle for correctness [https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866].

This work investigates whether a rigorously preregistered, verifier‑grounded paired experiment can detect meaningful differences between a deterministic template baseline and an LLM generator when both are evaluated by the same deterministic validator. We preregistered the experimental design (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3...) and archived all execution artifacts, provider traces, and validator outputs to permit exact reproduction (execution/execution_manifest.json). The preregistration froze the primary estimand: the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline across N = 120 paired tasks. Critically, the confirmatory generation semantics were preregistered as shared_initial_candidate: a single canonical candidate per task pair was generated and scored under both conditions. We explain why this choice—transparent in the preregistration—produced a degenerate but artifact‑correct confirmatory outcome and then provide runnable, artifact‑grounded remedies that enable informative independent comparisons.
sections.related_work:
Recent LLM→NetOps literature explores intent→configuration translation, generate–validate–repair workflows, and verifier grounding. Practical systems and testbeds have shown that verifier grounding materially improves deployment safety by catching semantic errors invisible to token‑level metrics [Batfish lessons; https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Several recent studies report LLM‑based configuration synthesis and intent translation benchmarks and emphasize the need for verification and iterative repair loops (examples: CN S M 2024 automation paper and intent‑based work cited in the preregistration list) [https://doi.org/10.23919/cnsm62983.2024.10814407, https://doi.org/10.1002/nem.70029].

Where prior work often publishes language metrics or ad‑hoc generate–validate loops without frozen estimands or exhaustive artifacts, our contribution is methodological: a frozen preregistered paired design with deterministic validator traces and a complete SHA‑256 manifest so auditors can rerun the exact experiment or the proposed alternative semantics. We do not claim broader production generality from these templated tasks; instead, we show how strict preregistration and complete artifact publication clarify what a confirmatory test actually measures and how to correct underpowered or semantically constrained assessments.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and operational artifacts. The complete preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; SHA‑256 7db1663cf3...) and execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) were frozen before any model calls. Key preregistered elements included: N = 120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class: edge, datacenter, multi‑AS); paired design; primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; confirmatory generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate"; maximum_model_calls = 240; declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da...); deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0) with scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The immutable initial master prompt used to orchestrate autonomous decisions is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

Task generation and templates. Tasks were synthesized by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (generator_version 5.0). Each task manifest entry (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, a required_sequence (explicit change steps that satisfy the intent safely), workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields or minimum_active_in_groups), allowed_touched_fields, and a difficulty annotation (changed_interface_count, transient_rule_count). Representative manifest entries and response files are archived in execution/responses and execution/scoring (examples: task‑000001 shared candidate at execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt SHA‑256 8f38c8be...). Templates intentionally encode operational safety constraints (make‑before‑break, atomic paired MTU change, etc.) so the validator evaluation has precise operational meaning.

Generation semantics and adapter. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter performed autonomous candidate generation via provider calls recorded under execution/provider_calls/*.json. The confirmatory run used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one canonical generation per pair (shared_initial) counted as the model call and reused for both baseline and guarded scoring. This choice isolates scoring behavior across conditions at the cost of removing independent generation variability as a source of difference. The complete provider traces and cached call artifacts (execution/call_cache/*.json) are published to permit reruns and alternative sampling.

Deterministic validator and scoring. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs: parsing and normalization of candidate commands; enforcement of per‑task workflow_policies (transient safety checks such as minimum_active_in_groups); computation of final_state and reachability invariants; and an explicit binary scoring outcome (VALID_CONFIGURATION = 1 when all required_commands and transient constraints are satisfied). Each scoring episode emits a JSON verifier trace archived under execution/scoring/*.json (representative: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1ad...). The validator records parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes (if any), and the final modeled device state.

Confirmatory analysis plan. The preregistered analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1. For each task i, baseline_i (binary) and guarded_i (binary) were recorded. The paired estimator is mean(guarded_i − baseline_i) across i = 1..120. Inference used a 10,000‑resample bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729) and exact McNemar two‑sided test. All analysis code and resampling seeds are archived (analysis/*). Contamination checks (exact match and n‑gram overlap heuristics) were preregistered and executed; results are stored in analysis/contamination_summary.csv.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw outcomes. Execution completed in scientific_confirmatory mode: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120 (shared_initial generation counted once per pair); full run manifest and per‑file SHA‑256s are in execution/execution_manifest.json. Confirmatory raw counts are:
- baseline_success_count = 120 of 120 (pass rate = 1.00)
- guarded_success_count = 120 of 120 (pass rate = 1.00)
The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 9f25790c...) is degenerate: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Representative scoring JSONs show identical canonical candidates and validator traces across conditions (examples archived: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt SHA‑256 8f38c8be..., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1ad...).

Statistical inference (preregistered). The paired estimator equals 0.00. The 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.00, 0.00]. The exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. These results are archived in analysis/results.json and summarized in analysis/condition_summary.csv (SHA‑256 9c77c96f...). The bootstrap distribution plot is archived as analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg (SHA‑256 ae5b8e0c...).

Representative validator diagnostics. Validator traces for sample tasks (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json, task-000002-guarded.json, task-000003-guarded.json) include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, validation_before and validation_after states, and violation_count = 0. For task‑000001 the validator reports required_command_count = 4 and final modeled state matching expected_final_state; for task‑000003 the validator reports required_command_count = 6 for a paired MTU change pattern. These concrete traces substantiate that the canonical candidates satisfied the template‑encoded workflows and transient constraints.

Contamination checks. Preregistered string‑overlap heuristics flagged no confirmatory contamination under the pre‑specified thresholds; the absence of flags is recorded in analysis/contamination_summary.csv. Full provider call traces and call_cache artifacts are published so independent auditors can reapply alternative exposure heuristics.
sections.discussion:
What the confirmatory result measures. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally evaluated a single canonical candidate under both baseline and guarded scoring episodes; the artifact traces show identical candidate strings and identical validator outcomes. Consequently the confirmatory paired test correctly reports no difference but does not probe independent LLM generative reliability. The artifacts make this transparent: the shared candidate files (execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt) and their identical SHA‑256 fingerprints (for many pairs) demonstrate that generation variability was not part of the confirmatory contrast.

Operational interpretation and recommended reruns. For operational deployment decisions the relevant quantity is the independent per‑condition pass probability of stochastic LLM generation. To estimate this with the same deterministic reproducibility guarantees, practitioners should rerun the included scoring harness with one of the artifact‑anchored modifications we published:
1) independent_per_condition confirmatory sampling: generate independent candidates per condition per task (e.g., seed_0 baseline, seed_1 guarded) and re‑run deterministic_netops_validator_v5. This change is runnable immediately using the published generation and scoring code and preserves exact reproducibility because all provider traces and seeds are archived. 2) multi‑seed confirmatory design: generate K ≥ 3 independent seeds per condition per task and compute per‑condition pass probabilities with bootstrapped paired contrasts. 3) validator diversification: include an orthogonal verifier (e.g., an emulation‑based reachability checker) and report intersection and union pass rates to mitigate validator–template coupling.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the preregistered shared_initial design removed generation variability, creating a degenerate paired outcome; this choice is disclosed and archived. Construct validity: template‑encoded required_sequences create strong alignment between templates and validator checks that may overstate performance relative to open natural intents. External validity: single model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic templates limit generalization. Conclusion validity: degenerate contingency tables yield correct but uninformative inferential results about independent generation; bootstrapped CI degeneracy reflects this. Each of these threats and their artifact evidence are recorded in execution/scoring/*.json and analysis/*.csv and must be considered when interpreting the confirmatory outcome.

Practical implications. The experiment demonstrates two operational points: (a) deterministic verifiers and explicit workflow_policies permit precise, reproducible correctness checks and are essential components of any NetOps automation pipeline; and (b) preregistration choices about generation semantics (shared vs independent) crucially determine whether confirmatory tests measure validator consistency or independent generator reliability. For practitioners, the lesson is operational: pair deterministic verifiers with independent per‑condition sampling when the objective is to assess stochastic generative reliability; use shared_candidate semantics only when the question is whether scoring machinery treats identical artifacts differently across conditions.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, verifier‑grounded paired experiment and released a complete artifact bundle enabling byte‑level reproduction (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics both the deterministic template baseline and the recorded gpt‑5‑mini guarded candidate validated on all N = 120 tasks (both 120/120). Archived traces demonstrate that identical canonical candidates per pair and template‑tight task constraints produced the degenerate paired outcome; consequently the confirmatory paired result does not provide evidence about independent LLM generative reliability. We provide artifact‑grounded, immediately runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory execution, validator diversification, task heterogeneity expansion) that preserve reproducibility and address the operational question of independent generative reliability. All execution and analysis artifacts—including the immutable master prompt reference (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and the preregistration SHA‑256—are included in the submission bundle to permit exact audit and follow‑up experiments. Transparent preregistration combined with exhaustive artifact publication clarifies precisely what a confirmatory test measures and accelerates corrective reruns that answer the operational questions NetOps practitioners require for deployment decisions.

limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: programmatic templates produced narrow required_sequences and workflow_policies that favour canonical solutions and limit external generalizability to heterogeneous operational intents.

Confirmatory shared_initial semantics: the preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' supplied identical canonical candidates to both conditions per pair, reducing independence between conditions and causing the degenerate paired outcome.

Single canonical seed for confirmatory test: the primary analysis used one canonical seed per task; preregistered exploratory multi‑seed analyses (seeds_1..4) were not included in the confirmatory inference reported here.

Validator–task coupling: the deterministic validator enforces constraints encoded in the task templates, which can increase pass rates for template‑aligned candidates and reduce construct validity for open distributions.

Possible training‑data exposure: preregistered contamination heuristics found no flags under chosen thresholds, but absence of a flag is not proof of zero exposure to related artifacts in model pretraining.

Single‑model, single‑validator run: results apply only to gpt‑5‑mini under the recorded configuration and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; they do not generalize across model families, agentic pipelines, or other validators.
